items.q: My grandmother (A) has lived in the same village (B) for forty years before she (C) finally moved to the city (D) with us last spring.
items.explanation: An action completed before another past action (she moved) takes the past perfect, not the present perfect: had lived.

items.q: The number of students (A) who are interested in joining the science club (B) have grown steadily (C) since the new laboratory (D) was opened last year.
items.explanation: The number of + plural noun is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular: has grown.

items.q: After the storm (A) had knocked down several power lines, the electricity (B) was cut off, so we ate dinner (C) by candlelight and went to (D) the bed early.
items.explanation: In the fixed expression go to bed (like go to school, go to work) no article is used before the noun.

items.q: (A) Rice farmers in the Mekong Delta (B) have always (C) depended of the yearly floods, (D) which bring rich soil and fresh fish to their fields.
items.explanation: The verb depend is always followed by the preposition on (depend on something), never of.

items.q: The scientist gave a (A) fascinating talk about how bees (B) communication with each other by dancing, and (C) even the youngest children (D) listened carefully.
items.explanation: After the subject bees a verb is needed, not a noun: bees communicate with each other.

items.q: The teacher asked Mai and (A) I to collect the notebooks (B) which had been left (C) on the desks and put them (D) in the cupboard.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of asked, so the object form is needed: the teacher asked Mai and me.

items.q: Although the new stadium is (A) much larger (B) than the old one, many fans say the atmosphere is (C) more worse because the seats are (D) far from the pitch.
items.explanation: Worse is already the comparative of bad, so it cannot take more as well.

items.q: If we (A) had left the house ten minutes earlier, we (B) would catch the last bus and (C) wouldn't have had to walk home (D) in the rain.
items.explanation: This is a third conditional about the unreal past (If + past perfect), so the main clause needs would have + past participle.

items.q: (A) When I phoned the hotel, the receptionist said that they (B) didn't have any rooms left (C) that night but that she (D) will call me if someone cancelled.
items.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb (said), will shifts back to would.

items.q: The old lighthouse, (A) that was built by French engineers in 1890, still guides fishing boats (B) safely into the harbour (C) on foggy nights, (D) although it has no keeper.
items.explanation: A non-defining relative clause (between commas) cannot begin with that; use which for a thing.

items.q: The tourists asked the guide (A) politely (B) whether the museum (C) was open on Mondays and (D) how much did the tickets cost.
options: how much did the tickets cost
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb and no auxiliary did is used: how much the tickets cost.

items.q: Before the chemistry exam, our teacher (A) reminded us to (B) do attention to the safety rules, (C) especially when (D) heating liquids over a flame.
items.explanation: The correct collocation is pay attention to something; do does not go with attention.

items.q: There were (A) so many people at the night market that we could (B) hardly move, and there was (C) very few space to sit down and (D) enjoy our food.
items.explanation: Space here is an uncountable noun, so it takes little, not few, which is used only with plural countable nouns.

items.q: (A) Despite the weather forecast promised sunshine, it rained (B) heavily all afternoon, (C) so the school sports day (D) had to be moved to the following week.
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause with a subject and verb needs the conjunction Although.

items.q: When he was young, my grandfather (A) is used to walk five kilometres to school, (B) even in the rainy season, because there (C) were no buses (D) in the area.
items.explanation: A past habit that no longer happens is expressed with used to + infinitive; be used to means be accustomed to and takes an -ing form.

items.q: Scientists (A) have known for many years that dolphins (B) use sound to find food, but nobody (C) has discovered exactly how they do it (D) until last year.
items.explanation: A finished time expression (until last year) requires the past simple, not the present perfect: nobody discovered.

items.q: The match lasted almost two hours (A) under the burning sun, and (B) by the final whistle (C) every one of the players (D) were completely exhausted.
items.explanation: The subject is every one, which is singular; the plural noun after of does not change the verb: every one of the players was.

items.q: My cousin, who is studying to become (A) an engineer, says that (B) the mathematics is (C) the most useful subject she (D) has ever taken at school.
items.explanation: School subjects and uncountable nouns used in a general sense take no article: mathematics is, not the mathematics.

items.q: We (A) arrived to the airport two hours early, (B) checked in our luggage and then (C) spent the rest of the time (D) looking at the planes through the huge windows.
options: spent the rest of the time
items.explanation: Arrive takes at for a building or place (arrive at the airport) and in for a city or country, never to.

items.q: The new smartphone app helps farmers (A) to check the weather, (B) compare prices at different markets and (C) sell their crops (D) more quick than before.
items.explanation: A word describing how the crops are sold modifies the verb, so an adverb is needed: more quickly.

items.q: (A) As soon as the door opened, the dog (B) jumped off the sofa, ran across the room and wagged (C) it's tail so hard that it (D) knocked over a vase.
items.explanation: The possessive pronoun is its with no apostrophe; it's is short for it is.

items.q: Fansipan is (A) the higher mountain in Vietnam, and although a cable car now takes visitors (B) most of the way up, many hikers (C) still prefer (D) to climb on foot.
items.explanation: Comparing one mountain with all the others in a country needs the superlative: the highest mountain in Vietnam.

items.q: Plants (A) cannot make their own food (B) unless they receive enough light, so a houseplant (C) will slowly die (D) if you will keep it in a dark corner.
items.explanation: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the present simple, not will: if you keep it in a dark corner.

items.q: (A) During the interview, the famous swimmer (B) said the reporters that she had trained six hours a day (C) since she was ten and (D) had never missed a session.
items.explanation: Tell takes a direct object (tell somebody something), while say does not: she told the reporters (or said to the reporters).

items.q: The village (A) where my grandparents live (B) has no internet connection, so my cousin, (C) who's phone never works there, (D) reads books all summer.
items.explanation: Possession in a relative clause is shown with whose; who's is short for who is or who has.

items.q: I (A) have never seen (B) a so beautiful sunset as the one we watched (C) from the beach (D) on our last evening in Phu Quoc.
items.explanation: Before a/an + adjective + noun the intensifier is such (such a beautiful sunset); so cannot follow the article.

items.q: Our history teacher says that the best way to (A) remember dates is (B) to link them (C) to a story, and her students usually (D) make good marks in exams.
items.explanation: The collocation is get (or achieve) good marks; make does not go with marks.

items.q: (A) Much of the students in our class (B) prefer to walk to school (C) rather than take the bus, (D) even when it is raining.
items.explanation: Students is a plural countable noun, so it takes many; much is used only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: (A) Both the players (B) and the coach (C) was surprised when the referee (D) stopped the game after only ten minutes because of lightning.
items.explanation: Both ... and joins two subjects into a plural subject, so the verb must be plural: both the players and the coach were surprised.

items.q: My parents (A) don't mind me playing games (B) at the weekend, but they (C) refuse letting me stay up (D) after midnight on school nights.
items.explanation: Refuse is followed by a to-infinitive, not an -ing form: refuse to let me stay up.
